description:
75 years ago, a historic winter storm known as the Great Appalachian Storm of 1950, The Storm of the Century, The Thanksgiving Blizzard, or the 1950 Superstorm wreaked havoc over the eastern third of the United States. It included a massive blizzard known in the Ohio Valley as The Big Snow, a huge sweeping cold front that plunged the South toward zero degrees, freezing rain that destroyed electric grids in central Pennsylvania, torrents of rain that flooded the midatlantic, and powerful winds that battered New England and caused storm surge along the Atlantic Coast.

Not only did millions of people suffer and hundreds die, but the storm became the most expensive storm in American history, and changed the science of storm prediction.

comments.text: “Imagine the psychological toll of being stranded in New Jersey.” 😂😂😂
comments.author: @davidkurvach3993

comments.text:
My dad remembered it taking him over 4 hours to cover the distance between Midland PA and Chester WV, a trip that normally takes about 20 minutes. He no so sooner got home and went to bed, when my granddad called for him to help shovel snow from the roof of the city hall and fire station since they were both volunteer firefighters at the time.
My great uncle had a small farm along US 30, just outside of Chester. He brought his sleigh and team of horses into town and helped deliver groceries to those who were snowed in.
My mom lived in Negley OH and was a high school student in nearby East Palestine. She remembered literally praying for the snow to last through the weekend so she could get a rare snow day from school.
comments.author: @leehuff2330

comments.text: My Father worked for Duquesne Light at  the time.  His best friend was shoveling snow at the main headquarters downtown when he died of a heart attack.  He was in his mid 30s.  I was born on July, 1949 (at Allegheny General Hospital) so I was too young to remember the storm but have pictures of me out in the snow with my Mother.   We lived in the Mexican War section of the Northside at the time (Resaca Place) which was completely covered with snow for days.  They both had some interestng stories of  walking a couple of miles after the storm to visit my grandparents to get them food.
comments.author: @frankschorr9145

comments.text: Dad was a 12 year old boy growing up in South Bend, Indiana in 1950.  He used to tell me about a big snow storm that made national news because it was so big and powerful.  This was likely that storm.  He showed me old pictures of the incredibly deep snow drifts and the weird looking snow formations on rooftops.  You did a great job with this story.
comments.author: @Jdwify

comments.text: I have a "created memory" of this storm.  I was about 30 months old.  We lived in Brackenridge, PA.  My parents told me that they placed me in the snow outside our home and it was as deep as I was tall.  I have formulated I mental picture of  "looking up" at the surface of the accumulated stnow.  I don't think I have actual memories of incidents from that age, hence the "created memory."  I spoke with a doctor who just barely made it home to Pittsburgh by car from medical school in Philadelphia.  At the end of the holiday weekend, he slogged more than a mile, through thigh high snow to reach a rail station for the return trip to Philadelphia by train.  A friend from Butler County left his dairy farm to travel by car to Elk County for opening day of deer season.  Although the snow was less in that region than southwestern PA,  he could not get closer that 2 miles from his camp.  He had to carry all his food and gear the rest of the way, making numerous crossings of Straight Creek on foot.  On two hours' sleep, he hunted all day - and worried about the possibility of more snow, returned home to relieve those who were tending to his cows that needed milking twice a day.

comments.text:
Thanks for this video. I have always remembered the ice storm in Altoona, Pa. when I was a boy, but could never remember the year. So this video shows it  was the Saturday after Thanksgiving, 1950. I was nine years old at that time, in the fourth grade at East End School on Kettle Road, Miss Martin teaching. 
I slept through it all, but my family said there was the sound of tree limbs breaking under the weight of ice all evening and most of the night. In front of our house on East Pleasant Valley Blvd., all the wires were down from all the poles as far as the eye could see. Mty parents had a coal furnace, as did many residents, so heat was not a problem. I seem to remember the power didn't come back on until close to Christmas. Of course we kids thought it was a lot of fun. My mother had candles and lamps going in several rooms.
The house across the boulevard from us (torn down when US220 was widened in 1959) had four big tall trees and most of their branches were stripped off and lying on the ground. Looking out my bedroom window I thoght that was pretty neat (awesome kids would say today.)
One thing about our neighborhood of East End in the 1950's. They used to put barricades up on some of the side streets so that we children could sled ride. That would be unheard of today. They did on Sheridan, the street by our house. Residents had to reach their garages on the alleys. Most garages were on the back alleys anyway. 
My sister, then 25, was pitching a fit, I was told by my family.  She was excitable. 
There was another time, when I was still a child, when it got darked than night during the day for a time during the warm weather months. The news said it was a fire in Canada but I don't remember the date on that either. 1949 maybe.
comments.author: @lloydstambaugh6918
